translations.text: A sermon for Holy Pascha by John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople.

Rejoice in the Lord always, beloved brothers. And again I say, rejoice. The Lord is near; be anxious about nothing. The Lord has risen from the dead, and with him a great multitude of saints. Let us therefore celebrate joyfully and chastely. For this is truly the day that the Lord has made. Let us rejoice and be glad in it.
Let us proclaim the remembrance of the day of salvation. Let us proclaim the resurrection of our Savior.
Above all, let us proclaim our salvation. Let us announce the putting to death of the devil, the captivity of the unclean demons,
the salvation of Christians, the resurrection of the dead. For through Christ’s resurrection fiery Gehenna will be extinguished, and the worm that never sleeps dies.
Hades is in turmoil. The devil mourns. Sin is put to death. Evil spirits are driven out. Those on earth ascend to heaven. Those in Hades are freed from the devil’s bonds.
and, taking refuge in God, they say to the devil, “Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O Hades, is your victory?”
Christ is the reason for this holy festival and celebration of ours. He is also the mediator of all good things for us.
For he created us in the beginning, bringing us from nonexistence into existence.
He has now also saved us when we were perishing, brought us to life when we were dead, and the enemy’s opposition
he has taken away. When we were slaves to sin, he made us free, wiping out our written record of debt.

“Christ,” it says, “redeemed us from the curse of the law, becoming a curse for us.” Therefore we too ought to say, “What shall I give back to the Lord for all that you have given us?” Being the only-begotten God,
he chose to become human for our sake and became obedient unto death, to deliver us from eternal death.
The Master of the angels clothed himself in the form of a servant. God the Word took flesh and appeared as a human, being of the same form and nature as the Father.
He endured this to free us from unjust slavery and deliver us from ungodliness. For this reason he consented to suffer in the flesh,
the giver of our life. For this reason he was also buried, the source of immortality, so that he might give everlasting life to mortals.

And again, as he went about the earth doing good and healing human afflictions, our Lord Jesus Christ received an unworthy reward from the Jews who fought against God in return for his great goodness.
cleansed lepers, gave sight to the blind, and healed the lame.
He drove out demons. He raised Lazarus from the dead after four days. He fed five thousand with five loaves. He walked on the sea. He turned water into wine.

He healed the woman suffering from bleeding. He brought the synagogue ruler’s dead daughter back to life. He performed many other mysteries, [?] wonders. But the Jews, gripped by envy and jealousy, sometimes pelted the Lord with stones, and at other times tried to throw him down from the walls.
Finally they also brought him to the cross. But our Lord Jesus Christ did not imitate the malice of the blaspheming Jews.
Instead, he gave his back to blows, according to the prophet’s words, and his cheeks to slaps.
And he did not turn his face away from the shame of being spat upon. Finally, he was led like a sheep to slaughter.

And like a lamb silent before its shearer, he did not resist or argue. When reviled, he did not revile in return; when suffering, he did not threaten. Instead, he entrusted himself to the one who judges justly. For at his first coming he did not come to torment and punish unbelievers.
but wished through patience and endurance to guide those who had gone astray to the truth.

And recognize the Lord’s great goodness. The Jews reviled him and said to him, “You have a demon.” But the Lord, being patient, drove out demons. The Jews spat in the Lord’s face, but he healed their blind. The Jews stoned Christ, but Christ gave their lame the ability to run. In every way he continued doing good to those who mistreated him, giving good in return for evil to those ungrateful and defiled people. He meekly endured slanders and was considered weak, though he received honor from angels. But lest I prolong my speech, let us come to the heart of the matter. Finally, the glorious King was led to the cross and to death, and he who is glorified by the cherubim and seraphim was nailed to the wood.
And he receives worship from all the angelic powers. He meekly accepted these things and suffered, giving us an example and becoming a teacher of meekness.

For this reason we too must endure the threats of evil people. Yet even when he was hanging on the cross, he displayed greater works and more numerous miracles, so that at least in this way he might restrain the madness of those hateful to God, leaving them no excuse for unbelief, nor allowing them to say, “We crucified a mere man.” First, then, Christ endured crucifixion so that he might drive away the demons in the air. He was hung on wood so that through wood he might heal humanity’s ancient sin. He was also pierced in the side with a spear because of the woman taken from Adam’s side. For the serpent deceived Eve, and Eve caused Adam to transgress, and a sentence was pronounced against them both. Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned. For this reason his side was pierced, so that we might know that Christ’s suffering brought salvation not only to men but also to women. For Adam was formed first,

and then Eve. And Adam was not deceived, but the woman fell into disobedience. Yet she will be saved through childbearing. Through what childbearing? Is it not through the birth of Mary’s child? For she bore Christ the Savior without having been with a man, as Isaiah bears witness, but with the Holy Spirit overshadowing her, as the archangel Gabriel announced. For this reason, then, the side

of Christ is pierced, so that what was foretold might come to pass, and the mysteries of baptism and the grace that was about to shine forth might be proclaimed. For blood and water flowed from Christ’s side, so that he might wipe away the record of our sins, and we might be cleansed by his blood and receive [?]. O great mystery! The robber repented. [?] water to be found so that he might be baptized.

He was hanging on the cross. There was no means of baptism at all: no spring, no lake, no rain, and no one to offer prayers. All the disciples had fled for fear of the Jews. Yet it was not that Jesus lacked water: even while hanging on the cross, he became the maker of waters. Since the thief could not enter the kingdom of heaven without baptism, and since, having repented, he ought not to be deprived of baptism, the Savior made water and blood flow from his pierced side, both to free the thief from the evils besetting him and to show that his blood had become redemption for those who put their hope in him. For if the blood of bulls and goats and the sprinkled ashes of a heifer sanctify those who are defiled, cleansing their flesh, how much more has the blood of Christ our Savior become cleansing for all Christians! If one of the unbelievers says to you, ‘Why was Christ crucified?’ tell him:
‘To undo through a tree the sin that arose in the human race.’
If he says to you, ‘Why, then, did he also wear thorns?’
Tell him, ‘To uproot Adam’s thorns and thistles. For he was condemned to groan and tremble, and thorns
and to produce thorns and thistles. But Jesus, who loves humankind, wishing to care for his creation,
suffered everything for our sake, so that we might be free from condemnation.
Just as he was born of a woman to wash away the sin that had come upon humanity, so also he was crowned with thorns,
to make the earth, which had been badly cultivated by sin, gentler through his obedience.
If he says to you, ‘Why did he drink gall and vinegar?’ tell him, ‘So that we might vomit out the serpent’s deadly poison. For that gall became sweetness and healing for us.’

If the unbeliever again says to you, ‘Why did they approach him and kneel before him?’ tell him, ‘So that the Jews might bow before him even unwillingly and proclaim his kingship on earth against their will. Now they bow before him in mockery, not knowing what they were doing.’
But at the coming resurrection every knee will bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth,
and every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. Amen.”
That cloak also has another symbolic meaning. It represented not only kingship, but also revealed the bloodthirstiness and murderousness of the Jews.
They also put a reed in his hand,
so that their sins might be written down. These things the enemies of God did, not recognizing the one being crucified—or rather, having willingly blinded themselves.
Creation, however, did not recognize its own builder and maker.
For while the Savior was hanging on the cross, the visible sun saw Christ, the sun of righteousness, being insulted by lawless men, but enduring

their insolence, it fled, darkening the earth, since it was unlawful to give light to the eyes of those committing such immense lawlessness. Not only did the sun flee, but the earth also shook, unable to endure that lawlessness of the Jews, showing and teaching that the one being crucified was God. Therefore it could not endure it, but was indignant, unwilling to carry upon itself the Jews whom God detested. For Cain did not so defile the earth when he killed his brother, nor did the giants’ building of the tower so burden the earth, nor did the Sodomites so defile it with their wrongdoing, nor did the [?] themselves, who made idols out of it.

Nor had the blood of Zechariah weighed it down so heavily, since the Jews committed this great impiety. For this reason even the hard rocks split apart, so that they might know that he is the spiritual and living rock. For it says, “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.” Oh, the senselessness of the Jews! The rocks split apart, yet they do not perceive it. Lifeless things move, yet those who have souls do not believe. The temple curtain was torn so that its desolation might be revealed. For the curtain was torn, and the things within the temple were laid bare, in accordance with Christ’s words: “Behold, your house is left to you desolate.” For everything held in honor among the Jews became desolate because of the killing of Christ. And the angels who dwelt in the city and in the temple departed from there and went into the Church. And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose with Christ, so that we might know that Christ, having died, would not rise alone, but would raise all
who place their hope in him.

This is the honored firstfruits, the feast of Easter, and these are the mysteries for Christians. We celebrate the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Therefore let us celebrate, not with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of purity and truth, believing in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, in the Trinity, of one essence and uncreated; believing in the resurrection; awaiting the Lord’s coming again, no longer humble but glorious, with heavenly splendor, with radiant angels, with a trumpet, with fear and joy—joy for the saints and the righteous, but fear for the unrighteous and sinners. May the God of peace for all make us worthy of the resurrection of the saints, through good deeds [?] and true faith. For to him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
